desk.headline: HEPS up 11% to 720c and interim dividend up 11% to 375c; spending seen staying constrained
results: Revenue rose 7.2% to R5.2bn: merchandise sales grew 3.9% to R2.6bn and other revenue (finance charges, insurance and services) grew 10.9% to R2.6bn.
Gross margin improved to 41.8% from 41.0%, at the top end of the 40–42% target; operating profit rose 10.1% to R575m, a 22.0% margin.
HEPS rose 11.2% to 720c (from 648c) and EPS 11.0% to 687c; the interim dividend rose 11.3% to 375c.
Credit sales grew 4.5% and were 70.7% of merchandise sales; the debtors book grew 11.8% and the collection rate improved to 79.2% from 78.3%.
The store base passed 1,000 (1,006 after a net 30 openings); net borrowings rose to R1.81bn from R1.48bn, gearing 50.7%.

guidance.summary: No earnings forecast. Lewis expects household spending to stay under pressure for some time and says it is well placed to beat its target of 40 new stores this financial year.

points: CEO Johan Enslin said demand for goods and in-store credit held up and called the debtors' book healthy.
Lewis rejected far more credit applications (45.7% declined vs 41.2%), which it linked to strict lending rules and rising consumer stress.
Sales picked up in the second quarter: merchandise sales grew 5.0% versus 2.7% in the first quarter.
Higher fuel and transport costs, high unemployment and political and fiscal uncertainty were flagged as pressures on customers.
Promotions across all brands are planned for Black Friday and the festive season, backed by new ranges and good stock levels.
call.source: Results announcement and coverage: The National, 19 Nov 2026 (CEO comments); Business Explainer, 19 Nov 2026; Investing.com, 19 Nov 2026

watch: Black Friday and festive-season trading in a tight consumer market.
Credit quality: debtor costs grew 13.4%, faster than the book, and the decline rate is rising.
Store openings against the 40-store target and the level of borrowings by year-end.
